title: Queues: moving slow work out of the request
story:
A request arrives needing work that takes far longer than the caller will wait. Doing it inline holds a connection, a thread and the caller's attention for the whole duration, and under load those three run out in that order. The move is to accept the request, write down what needs doing, answer immediately, and let something else do it.

What that buys is a decoupling: the rate at which work arrives no longer has to equal the rate at which it is done. Bursts are absorbed rather than rejected, the worker can be scaled independently of the thing taking requests, and a failure in the slow part stops being a failure of the fast part.

What it costs is that you now own a queue, and queues obey an arithmetic that is worth knowing exactly. Little proved it in 1961: in a queuing process, where the mean time between arrivals of two consecutive units is one over lambda, L is the mean number of units in the system and W is the mean time spent by a unit in the system, then given finiteness and stationarity conditions, L equals lambda times W. The remarkable part is its indifference — the relationship is not influenced by the arrival process distribution, the service distribution, the service order, or practically anything else, and it applies to systems within systems as readily as to the whole.

Read it as the diagnostic it is. The number of items sitting in your queue equals the arrival rate multiplied by the time each spends in the system. So a queue that is growing is not telling you that it is busy; it is telling you that arrival rate exceeds service rate, and that gap will not close by itself. Adding queue capacity does not help — it converts a fast failure into a slow one, letting the backlog grow until the wait is useless and then failing anyway, with more work lost.

Three consequences follow for design. The caller needs a way to learn the outcome, because the immediate answer was only an acknowledgement — which means a status endpoint, a callback, or a notification, and that is work you did not have to do when the answer was inline. Messages can be delivered more than once, so the handler has to be idempotent, which is the previous lesson arriving as a requirement rather than a suggestion. And something must decide what happens to messages that fail repeatedly, because a message that cannot be processed and is retried forever is a worker that does nothing else — which is what a dead letter queue exists to prevent.

problem.name: Asynchronous work
problem.shape: A request needs work that takes far longer than the caller is willing to wait for.
tell: a request handler performs work measured in seconds or minutes
bursts of traffic exhaust connections or threads
a slow downstream dependency makes the whole endpoint slow
a queue's depth is rising and nobody can say why
problem.move: Accept the request, record the work as a message, acknowledge immediately, and process separately. Then give the caller a way to learn the outcome, make the handler safe to run more than once, and decide in advance where messages go when they fail repeatedly. Watch queue depth as a rate mismatch rather than as a capacity figure.
problem.invariant: The mean number of items in the system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the mean time each spends in it, independently of the arrival distribution, the service distribution and the service order.
problem.breaks: A queue absorbs bursts and cannot absorb a sustained rate mismatch. Where arrivals exceed service indefinitely, extra capacity only delays the failure and enlarges it — the backlog grows until the wait exceeds the work's usefulness, and then the failure arrives with more work in it.

cost.time: the caller gets an acknowledgement rather than an answer, so the outcome has to be delivered some other way
cost.space: the backlog itself, plus stored state for tracking each item's fate
cost.beats: doing the work inline, which holds connections for the duration and fails the whole request when the slow part fails

worked.problem: Your queue depth is growing. What is it telling you?
worked.reasoning:
That arrivals are exceeding service, and that no amount of queue capacity will fix it — a growing queue is a rate problem wearing a storage costume.

The arithmetic says so directly. The mean number of items in the system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the mean time each item spends there. If depth is rising while arrival rate is steady, then time-in-system is rising, which means service is not keeping up. The relationship holds regardless of the arrival distribution, the service distribution or the order work is done in, which is what makes it usable as a diagnostic rather than a model you have to fit.

So the first thing it rules out is the comforting interpretation. A rising queue does not mean the system is busy and will catch up. Catching up requires service rate to exceed arrival rate for a while, and nothing about the queue causes that to happen. If the rates are genuinely mismatched, the backlog grows without bound until something else breaks.

The second thing it rules out is the obvious remedy. Adding capacity to the queue does not address a rate mismatch — it converts a fast failure into a slow one. Work sits longer, the wait eventually exceeds the point at which the result is useful, and then you fail anyway with far more work lost than if you had shed load at the door.

So the real responses are about rates. Raise service rate: more workers, faster handlers, batching where the work amortises. Lower arrival rate: shed load, rate-limit, reject at the edge, which is the next lesson. Or reduce time-in-system directly by doing less per item.

Two diagnostics I would want before choosing. Whether the mismatch is a burst or sustained, because a queue is the right tool for the first and the wrong one for the second — and the way to tell is to look at whether depth returns to baseline between peaks. And whether the backlog is one poisoned message being retried forever, which presents as a growing queue and is not a capacity problem at all; that is what a dead letter queue exists to catch, and its absence is why a single bad message can consume a worker indefinitely.

The framing I would offer is that queue depth is not a capacity measurement. It is the integral of a rate mismatch, and the only fix is on one of the two rates.

problem.practice: Graph queue depth alongside arrival rate and completion rate on one axis. Check whether depth returns to baseline between peaks. Then find your slowest handler and work out how many workers the current arrival rate requires — and what happens to depth if one worker dies.

beats.broke: A request arrives needing work that takes far longer than the caller will wait, and doing it inline holds a connection, a thread and the caller's attention for the whole duration.
beats.fix: Accept the request, record the work as a message, answer immediately, and let a separate worker perform it — decoupling the rate at which work arrives from the rate at which it is done.
beats.cost: The queue converts a slow response into a pending one, so the caller needs another way to learn the outcome — and any sustained mismatch between arrival and service shows up as an unbounded backlog rather than as an error.

interview.q: Your queue depth is growing. What is it telling you?
interview.trap: Reading it as busyness that will resolve, or adding queue capacity. Depth is the integral of a rate mismatch, so more capacity converts a fast failure into a slow one with more work lost — and the cause is sometimes one poisoned message rather than load at all.
